items.title: Ask HN: I have been unemployed for 2y. 15 years of experience, US. What to do?
items.content:
I'm Senior software engineer in the US (DMV area), with 15y of experience. Worked for Fortune 50+ company and bunch of mid-size companies. Been unemployed for 2y and can't find a job, within those 2 years, I pretty much spent my savings that I've saved through years, maybe have 4-5 months left to support my household. Currently, I tutor math and probably about to start working as manager in pizzaria.

In Jan 2025, I quit from a mid-size insurance tech company(1000+) after working there for almost 4y, because I was tipped off the they were about to start layoffs and they did. Well, since then I have zero luck finding any job in SWE.

At this point, I have massive gap in my resume that I can't explain to recruiters, I can still code (C#/.NET/AWS) and learned the AI, but who cares if date of my last employment is Jan2025. What should I do ?

If you have an alternative path (something completely different from SWE or SWE adjacent) that pays "well", I would like to hear.

items.title: Show HN: OpenComputer – an open source alternative to Devin
items.content:
Hi HN!

Utpal here, I'm one of the founders of OpenComputer.

OpenComputer is an open source cloud coding agent for teams that can run in your own cloud account (AWS, GCP, Azure).

We run the agent harness and the sandbox on the same durable VM (architecture in the docs [1]). First commit lands in 24s; the alternatives we benchmarked took 53-72s (benchmarks below [2]).

Two other choices:

- One VM per team, scalable horizontally. Sessions are isolated in git worktrees. - Session files are backed up to a repo after every turn, so any session can resume on another VM.

We noticed that past ~640 session-hours a month, one always-on 4 vCPU VM is cheaper than per-session E2B sandboxes, for example. So at scale, this setup would not only be faster than current SOTA coding agents, but also more cost-efficient.

Feel free to try via cloud for free [4] or self host. We would love any and all feedback, and happy to answer any questions! Full demo below [3].

[1]: https://docs.opencomputer.dev/getting-started/architecture [2]: https://opencomputer.dev/blog/cloud-agents-as-fast-as-local/ [3]: https://x.com/IgorZIJ/status/2121309785882591711 [4]: https://app.opencomputer.dev

items.title: Launch HN: Onlook (YC W25) – An open-source developer tool for designers
items.content:
Hey HN, I'm Daniel, founder of Onlook (https://github.com/onlook-dev/onlook and onlook.com).

Onlook is a desktop app that puts a canvas on top of your real codebase, letting you design directly in code with the agent you already use. Over 25,000 designers and developers have supported the project, 100+ have contributed, and it's been the #1 trending repo in the world twice. We just rebuilt the entire product as an agentic design tool, and open-sourced it to the community.

Here’s a demo video: (https://youtu.be/BogcYWf4siM)

If you're an engineer, traditional engineering tools are largely built for convergence, whereas designers tend to explore and diverge on ideas. Onlook gives designers a familiar canvas while managing all of the dev processes that get between them and making mind-blowing designs in code. Designers can work on a multiple simultaneous worktrees that run on the real app locally, and every change lands as a PR you can review or throw away, so there aren’t mockups to rebuild.

We built Onlook because we believe there needs to be a developer tool that works the way designers do.

More and more, designers are expected to work in code. Designers think by seeing, drafting, arranging variations, using references, and remixing ideas. That’s why the canvas has been the signature feature of design tools because it genuinely is useful for how messy the creative process is. Most of the challenge of using engineering tools for design work is that the first half of starting a project often takes mental bandwidth in of itself (What branch am I on? What page was that last exploration on?) and the second half is constrained by configuring your coded design to present itself (prompting design tools on top of what you’ve built or making temporary navigation for that specific state).

Some of you may remember our earlier Show HNs (July 2024: https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=40904862, August 2024: https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=41390449, May 2025: https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=44127653). Since then, we built a web version (too early), then a Storybook-native build (a mistake). We noticed that our desktop product from July 2024 was still getting hundreds of downloads a month despite zero promotion, so we decided to rebuild it for the new era of designers working in code.

How it works…

Onlook shines at exploring tons of ideas at once. Ask it to lay out every flow in your product, show every state of a component, or riff on ten versions of one screen. Your designs all show up side by side on an infinite canvas, with each frame as a real webview running your actual app with real data. Not as a mockup, but the real deal.

When we built this editor, we had an epiphany that it could be a new kind of IDE for design. Design tools used to be limited to a proprietary setup or closed schema, but now you can push and pull the medium of code to get whatever result you want, so why not give agents an infinite canvas of browsers and see what they do? It turns out, the agents can figure out how to better present coded work by adjusting the urls of browser frames and arranging and resizing them on the canvas.

The concept is simple, but it requires a lot of product thinking. For example, because all of the frames on the canvas share a single browser session, and Chromium only allows six connections per host per session, ten frames of the same app end up fighting over limited connections. So, we had to plan around that, and there are still tons of things we need to do to make the canvas ultra performant.

Onlook is an Electron app where you can import a repo from GitHub or upload a local folder. Then, Onlook creates a git worktree, starts your dev server, and has the agent sort out missing dependencies or other requirements. You never open a terminal and everything the agent does is a normal git diff that can go to GitHub as a PR. We inject a small script into each frame that draws selection outlines and reads the page, so that way you can click an element, say "make this a card layout," and the agent knows exactly what "this" is.

This time we didn't build our own agent. Onlook runs Claude Code or Codex on your own subscription, and we turn whatever the agent emits into one typed event log and draw the UI from that in our own chat interface. On top of that we give the agent a bespoke set of design-specific tools, from arranging frames on the canvas, to making suggestions, to generating multiple iterations of a selection – which is especially useful because the agent decides how to get the app into a state that you need based on your prompt.

We also have our own Artifacts which are quick HTML sketches that live in the editor, but outside your repo. They’re almost like components in other design tools in that they can be carried and edited across every project but are detached from the project with no network access. As an example, you can ask the agent to turn your interface into an Artifact, and use it as a reference for another exploration, or download it as HTML and send it to a coworker as an interactive export of something you have in progress. I frequently go back to the artifacts I’ve made as visual snippets when I need new ideas or need to borrow something that’s already been built.

The desktop editor is free (you can download it from our website at onlook.com) and open source under Apache-2.0, and we'll eventually offer a paid cloud product for teams.

We'd lov

items.title: Show HN: Fast deterministic natural language search for OpenStreetMap data
items.content:
I want to show you HippoMaps. It is a fully featured map and navigation app built on OpenStreetMap with a custom Overpass API engine for really fast search of POIs, areas and ways.

My aim with HippoMaps is to get to a level where I don't need Google Maps anymore. The biggest hurdle IMHO with OSM based apps is the lack of nice and fast search (where GMaps excels at). To get there I started working on a deterministic (as in no LLMs used) parser of queries that translates them to the Overpass QL.

Search queries are split into tokens and the algorithm tries to guess "what" you want to search and "where". The former comes from a word list (known brands, sports, OSM tags) and the latter from the geocoder service (Photon).

You can get quite creative like "cafes in Zurich by the Limmat", "peaks over 4000 m in Valais", "pharmacies open now in Bern". It's good for discovering hiking trails, e.g. "hiking trails from Arth-Goldau to Rigi Kulm". It knows how to find stuff between two places, next to a place, near a place and so on. You can stack those as well like "bridges over the danube in serbia 50 km from novi sad".

Except the search it has almost all of the features you would expect from a map like turn-by-turn navigation (Valhalla) with voice (Piper), public transport navigation in Europe (MOTIS), live traffic (only a few countries so far).

The app is GPL-3.0: https://github.com/cdutsov/hippomaps

I'm looking forward to feedback on searches that work or don't work for you + overall comments.

items.title: Show HN: Foolscap – a writing app that reads your book and never writes for you
items.content:
People are scared of their ability to write and think atrophying, so I wondered: what if I built something that enhanced human creativity instead of destroying it by doing the thinking and writing for people? Foolscap is the result, or at least the first version of that idea that's fleshed out enough to share here.

It reads as you write and picks out the structure: characters, ideas, threads, what's left hanging. You can respond to what it picks out, so there's a dialectic between the system and you as the writer. There's also an agent on the side, plugged into the same system, so you can ask about your book and fire off actions through conversation. It never writes into your work.

The system can also follow theorems and proofs and string together their dependencies, but I haven't made that a focus yet. There's no Lean support, for example. If anyone's interested in that, I'd love to hear it.

I want to build this by iterating with the people who use it: a tool that uses AI not to bypass the creative process, but to bring new tools to it. There's a free tier, and if you email hello@foolscap.works I'll send you a code for 50% off. This is my first product, so feedback of any kind is welcome.

Thanks, David
